newsitem.title: USA: IMF offers Philippines $1.1 billion after crash.
newsitem.headline: IMF offers Philippines $1.1 billion after crash.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund offered the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support on Friday to help ease the problems caused by a currency crash.

The loan, $699 million of it to be available immediately, extended $652 million from an existing three-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) credit line until the end of this year and added $435 million of extra cash, the IMF said in a statement.

The statement said the Philippines authorities promised to keep interest rates high until the foreign exchange market stabilised and to back their exchange rate policy with strong fiscal and monetary policies.

"The size of financial support that is being made available is quite modest, but it is all that is seen as necessary in the circumstances," said an international monetary source, who asked not to be identified.

Manila asked the IMF for help after it was forced to let the peso float following strong speculative pressure. The peso has fallen almost 12 percent since the float and authorities have set up a special hotline to allow individuals to report merchants who jack prices up to boost their profits.
Manila bankers expect the peso to recover slightly next week.

The $1.1 billion credit line was made available under special fast-track regulations drawn up after the Mexico crisis of early 1995. These rules aimed to let the IMF respond quickly to financial problems and kick in when experts think a crisis is in the cards.

"In approving the request of the Philippines for an extension and augmentation of the EFF, the IMF made use, for the first time, of the accelerated procedures established under the Emergency Financing Mechanism (EFM)," the IMF said.

"The EFM was adopted in September 1995 to strengthen the IMF ability to respond swiftly in support of a member country facing an external financial crisis and seeking assistance from the IMF in support of a strong macroeconomic programme."
The IMF said it expected the Philippines economy to grow by 6.3 percent this year, up from 5.7 percent in 1996. Consumer price inflation would fall to 6.5 percent, from 8.4 percent in 1996.
"The performance of the Philippines economy under the EFF-supported programme has been satisfactory," the IMF said.
"Real GDP growth accelerated... Inflationary pressures were kept under control and net international reserves increased to the equivalent of 2.8 months of imports."
Thailand's currency crisis triggered that in Manila. However, Thailand has taken a different path from that taken by Manila and ministers say they will not be seeking IMF support.

"They are going along a different track, and that probably reflects the political realities within the country," the monetary source said. "The Philippines already had a long-standing relationship with the IMF and their reaction was to hunker down again and get something sorted out."
